title: Hiding in Plain Sight: the Potential of Christian Higher Education
author: Elizabeth Stice
summary: Elizabeth Stice, a 2026 fellow of the Center for Christianity and Public Life, compares the new publicly funded civic thought centers at universities such as Florida, Texas Austin, and Ohio State with the existing network of Christian liberal arts colleges. She credits the civic centers with correctly seeing that education shapes the civic imagination, but notes their political origins and the way they compete with starved departments. Christian colleges already teach Antigone, Crito, Augustine, Plato, and Hobbes alongside Scripture, producing graduates who bring Christian resources into public life. Yet most are tuition-dependent and many are closing, and she observes that her own university has not one endowed chair in history or honors. Her argument is that supporters of the Christian imagination do not need to found new centers; they need to fund the ones that already exist, for example through endowed liberal arts chairs across CCCU schools.
points: The new civic thought centers recognize that funding courses on the founding and the Great Books shapes the civic imagination, but their political origins and funding create friction on campus.
Christian liberal arts colleges already function as small centers for the Christian imagination, with students reading Locke and Leviticus and Rousseau and Romans.
With over 500,000 CCCU students, the Christian liberal arts tradition is a large but under-resourced channel for civic virtue.
Many tuition-dependent Christian colleges are closing, and some have no endowed chair in history or honors at all.
The practical conclusion is to fund existing Christian institutions through endowed liberal arts chairs rather than to found new centers.
quotes: Funding faculty, courses, and programming on the American founding or diplomacy or the Great Books gives college students the opportunity to seize hold of these stories and ideas for themselves.
In a sense, each of them is a small center for the Christian imagination. Each of them is an incubator for future Christian leaders, equipped both spiritually and academically.
The Christian liberal arts tradition is especially valuable for civic life.
These are students who read Locke and Leviticus, Rousseau and Romans.
The flame of Christian imagination is burning, but it is not especially well fed. We have not one endowed chair in history or in honors at my university.

While others are pushing to found centers to cultivate civic thought and virtue, we already have institutions designed to cultivate Christian thought and virtue. We do not need to found them. We need to fund them.
